summaries.headline: Chicago Board Urges Governor to Reject Federal Choice Program
summaries.summary: The Chicago Board of Education voted 15-0 to denounce the Trump administration's tax credit scholarship program and ask Governor JB Pritzker to keep Illinois out of it. The federal program provides dollar-for-dollar tax credits up to $1,700 for donors who contribute to scholarship-granting nonprofits serving families earning up to 300% of local median income — roughly $233,000 for Chicago families. More than half of states have already opted in, with Pritzker still weighing the decision as some Democratic leaders like Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza embrace the program despite Chicago's opposition.

summaries.headline: Student Mental Health Needs Outpace District Response Systems
summaries.summary: District leaders face intensifying student mental health challenges that require systemic rather than programmatic solutions. A national survey found 58 percent of school-based providers reported worsening student mental health in 2025, up from 46 percent the previous year. The districts making progress focus on building consistent everyday systems — trusted adult relationships, clear routines, and early intervention pathways — rather than relying on single programs or departments to address complex behavioral needs.

summaries.headline: CoSN Conference Focuses on Collaborative Ed Tech Leadership
summaries.summary: Educational technology leaders will gather at the CoSN 2026 Annual Conference in Chicago April 13-15 under the theme "Building What's Next Together" to address collaborative approaches to future learning environments. The conference programming reflects CoSN's 2026 Driving K-12 Innovation report, which identifies staffing shortages, cybersecurity threats, and critical media literacy as the field's biggest challenges, while highlighting generative AI, data visualization, and privacy tools as priority technologies. The emphasis on superintendent-technology leader collaboration signals recognition that successful ed tech implementation requires alignment between district leadership and technical expertise rather than isolated technology initiatives.

summaries.headline: Ohio Revamps Reading Teacher Training After Research Gaps
summaries.summary: Ohio lawmakers launched a statewide science of reading initiative in 2023 after discovering that existing teacher preparation fell short of research-based standards. A 2023 NCTQ report found that only one-third of Ohio's elementary teacher preparation programs adequately covered all five components of reading science, while more than half promoted approaches contrary to evidence-based methods like phonics instruction. The state's focus on strengthening teacher training represents a critical shift toward research-backed reading instruction as districts work to address troublingly low reading scores.

summaries.headline: Chicago Board Urges Governor to Reject Federal School Choice Credits
summaries.summary: The Chicago Board of Education will vote Wednesday on a resolution asking Governor JB Pritzker to reject Trump administration efforts supporting private schools with public funds through a new federal tax-credit program. The program offers dollar-for-dollar tax credits up to $1,700 for donors giving to scholarship nonprofits, benefiting families earning up to 300% of local median income—roughly $233,000 annually in Chicago—while more than half of U.S. states have already opted in. Pritzker's decision puts Illinois among the final holdouts as even some Democratic governors reconsider their initial opposition to the program.

summaries.headline: Philadelphia Teachers Brace for $225 Million Budget Cuts
summaries.summary: Philadelphia educators are preparing for larger class sizes and reduced student support as district leaders advance a $225 million spending reduction that would eliminate 560 positions, including 220 building substitutes and 340 school-based roles like special education aides and climate staff. The cuts target support roles outside classrooms while the district faces a $300 million budget deficit, with teachers saying the plan has "decimated morale" and created deep anxiety about job placements. Teachers worry the reductions will push more behavioral and academic challenges into already strained classrooms at a time when many students and staff are still struggling with post-pandemic recovery needs.

summaries.headline: LAUSD Strike Exposes California's Structural Funding Crisis
summaries.summary: Nearly 70,000 LAUSD workers plan to strike April 14 as union contracts expire amid surging inflation and stagnant pay, with many classified staff unable to afford one-bedroom apartments in Los Angeles. The district faces a $191 million deficit, declining enrollment that shrinks per-pupil funding, and the end of pandemic relief dollars that temporarily masked deeper fiscal gaps. The impasse reflects a statewide pattern where districts across California are reaching similar breaking points, suggesting the crisis extends far beyond any single district's bargaining table.

summaries.headline: Hickory Partnership Tackles Literacy and Teacher Shortage Together
summaries.summary: Hickory City Schools has partnered with Lenoir-Rhyne University to address early literacy challenges while simultaneously building their teacher pipeline through an innovative collaboration at Southwest Primary School. University education students work directly in classrooms implementing science of reading practices, gaining hands-on experience while providing additional instructional support during critical literacy instruction. The model creates a sustainable cycle where future teachers receive high-quality preparation in evidence-based reading instruction while current students benefit from increased classroom capacity and expertise.

summaries.headline: Districts Need Cyber Readiness Roadmaps, Not Just Tools
summaries.summary: District technology leaders recognize cybersecurity as a critical concern but struggle to translate awareness into action due to limited budgets, small staffs, and competing priorities. CDW has developed a cybersecurity maturity assessment specifically designed for K-12 environments, using a school district interpretation of the National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework that accounts for the funding and staffing realities most districts face. The assessment helps districts understand their current security posture and prioritize next steps based on their actual resources rather than enterprise-level assumptions about capacity.

summaries.headline: Colorado Spares Schools From $1.2B Budget Cuts
summaries.summary: Colorado lawmakers avoided major cuts to K-12, early childhood, and higher education funding despite facing a $1.2 billion budget shortfall for 2026-27. The proposed $46.8 billion budget increases K-12 spending by $184 million to $10.2 billion statewide, while lawmakers focus cuts on Medicaid benefits and health programs instead of reviving the Budget Stabilization Factor that previously withheld constitutionally mandated school funding. The decision to tap state reserves and preserve education funding signals lawmakers' recognition that rebuilding from past education funding holes takes priority over immediate fiscal austerity.

summaries.headline: Public Universities Face April 2026 ADA Compliance Deadline
summaries.summary: Public colleges and universities must comply with new ADA Title II web accessibility regulations by April 24, 2026, requiring all digital content, websites, mobile apps, course materials, and virtual events to meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA technical standards. The U.S. Department of Justice has set specific accessibility requirements for the first time through regulation, covering state and local government entities including all public higher education institutions. Universities now have less than two years to audit and update their entire digital infrastructure, from student portals to online coursework, creating significant technical and budgetary pressures for already-stretched IT departments.

summaries.headline: States Push AI Privacy Rules Over Classroom Mandates
summaries.summary: State legislators introduced 134 artificial intelligence bills across 31 states this session, prioritizing student data protection and usage restrictions over widespread classroom adoption requirements. California's AB 1159 prohibits using student data to train AI models, while Idaho's SB 1227 requires statewide privacy frameworks and Oklahoma mandates human oversight for high-stakes student decisions. The legislative pattern suggests policymakers are building guardrails first rather than racing to integrate AI tools, reflecting cautious approaches to emerging technology in schools.

summaries.headline: Wisconsin Parents Underestimate School Spending by Wide Margins
summaries.summary: Wisconsin parents significantly underestimate per-pupil spending in their districts, with 44% saying they're "not sure" about funding levels and another 43% guessing below actual amounts. When informed of real spending figures, only 27% of parents say the amount is "too little," while the majority believe current funding is adequate or excessive. The knowledge gap emerges as voters face 74 spring referenda requests, suggesting that transparency about actual spending levels could reshape public support for additional school funding measures.

summaries.headline: Chicago CEO Keeps Schools Open Despite Board Support for Protest Day
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools interim CEO Macquline King announced schools will remain open May 1 despite pressure from the Chicago Teachers Union and a majority of board members to close for a nationwide day of protest against Trump administration policies. King said in her statement that if the board wants to cancel classes, members must convene a special meeting and take a formal vote "as soon as possible" to provide clarity for families. The standoff represents an early test of King's leadership as she navigates between union demands—backed by Mayor Brandon Johnson, a former CTU organizer—and her own recommendation to maintain instructional continuity.

summaries.headline: AI Literacy Tops Priorities But Training Lags
summaries.summary: Organizations identify AI literacy as their top learning priority while employees report lacking clarity on how artificial intelligence adoption will affect their roles and career progression, according to a new Docebo report. The disconnect suggests companies recognize the strategic importance of AI skills but haven't yet built the infrastructure to deliver meaningful training at scale. The gap between stated priorities and actual training delivery may leave workforces unprepared for AI integration across industries, including education technology roles that increasingly require AI fluency.

summaries.headline: Massachusetts Awards $4.3M for Secondary Literacy Programs
summaries.summary: Haverhill Public Schools and Greater Lawrence Regional Vocational Technical School received $213,000 and $194,000 respectively as part of more than $4.3 million in state grants to continue participation in the Partnership for Reading Success—Massachusetts (PRISM III) program. The funding, distributed between September and February through a mix of state and federal dollars, supports 16 districts and educational collaboratives in strengthening English language arts and literacy instruction for grades four through 12. The continuation grants signal Massachusetts' sustained investment in secondary literacy at a time when many districts struggle with older students who lack foundational reading skills needed for post-graduation success.

summaries.headline: Ellucian Hires Commercial Chief to Drive AI Growth
summaries.summary: Ellucian appointed Josh Rice as Chief Commercial Officer to lead global commercial operations as higher education institutions accelerate their shift to cloud-based systems and AI-powered platforms. Rice, a former Shopify vice president who previously held leadership roles at Workday, Google, Microsoft, and AWS, will oversee revenue, services, and customer success for the company that serves around 3,000 institutions globally. The hire signals intensifying competition among education technology vendors to position AI-enabled platforms at the center of campus operations as institutions seek integrated systems for student services, administration, and data-driven decision-making.

summaries.headline: Microsoft Partnership Pushes AI Agents Into Marketing
summaries.summary: Microsoft and Publicis Groupe expanded their decade-long partnership to build integrated AI systems that embed autonomous agents across marketing workflows, moving beyond standalone AI tools toward connected platforms. The collaboration combines Microsoft's Azure cloud infrastructure and AI capabilities with Publicis' data transformation services, allowing AI agents to operate across campaign planning, content generation, and performance optimization within unified systems. The shift signals how enterprise AI adoption is evolving from isolated applications to comprehensive platforms that can influence business operations and decision-making at scale.

summaries.headline: Springfield Attendance Drops After Threats Prompt Safety Sweeps
summaries.summary: Springfield City Schools has implemented daily safety sweeps across all buildings after a series of threats caused attendance rates to decline district-wide. The district now conducts comprehensive security checks each morning before classes begin, while working with local law enforcement to investigate the source of the threats that have disrupted normal operations. The attendance drops signal how quickly security concerns can undermine instructional time, forcing districts to balance visible safety measures with maintaining a learning environment that encourages students to show up.

summaries.headline: Military Families Receive 10,000 Literacy Kits
summaries.summary: USAA has partnered with United Through Reading to distribute 10,000 literacy kits to military families this month. The initiative targets families who face unique challenges with educational continuity due to frequent relocations and deployments that can disrupt traditional school-family literacy partnerships. The distribution recognizes how military children's academic success depends on maintaining literacy support across multiple school systems and geographic moves.

synthesis.topic_title: School Funding Battles Shift to Courtrooms as States Grapple with Formula Updates

The combination of rising operational costs and political gridlock over tax policy is pushing districts toward litigation as a funding strategy.

[Facebook](https://aldailynews.com/#facebook "Facebook") [Twitter](https://aldailynews.com/#twitter "Twitter") [Mastodon](https://aldailynews.com/#mastodon "Mastodon") [Email](https://aldailynews.com/#email "Email") [Share](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Faldailynews.com%2Falabama-lawmakers-finalize-12-4-billion-education-budget-package%2F&title=Alabama%20lawmakers%20finalize%20%2412.4%20billion%20education%20budget%20package)

BIRMINGHAM, Ala. – Alabama lawmakers on Tuesday finalized the state’s education spending plan for next year, after the House agreed to Senate changes.

Lawmakers signed off on a [$10.5 billion FY27 Education Trust Fund budget](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/RBPXJNM-1.pdf), [a $420 million supplemental appropriation](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB235-enr.pdf) available to spend during the current fiscal year, and a separate [$1 billion Education Advancement and Technology Fund](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB236-enr.pdf) allocation also available to spend during the current fiscal year.

In the main FY27 ETF budget, lawmakers included $86.25 million for CHOOSE Act education savings accounts – $85 million for education savings account awards and $1.25 million for the Department of Revenue to administer them.

The supplemental bill also includes a separate $100 million appropriation from the CHOOSE Act Fund to the Department of Revenue, money available to pay ESA awards for the 2026-27 school year.

The final ETF budget also includes a 2% pay raise for educators and a conditional $32.9 million appropriation for a one-time bonus for retired educators.

Lawmakers tweaked the RAISE Act weights used to allocate additional funding to help students facing certain challenges. The poverty weight increased from 2.25% to 2.75%, the Tier I special education weight rose from 2% to 2.5%, and the gifted student weight increased from 4.5% to 4.75%. Other weights, including those for English learners and higher tiers of special education, remained unchanged.

The $420 million [supplemental appropriation](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB235-enr.pdf) provides one-time spending for the current fiscal year, sending money to K-12 and higher education programs, school safety and technology needs along with a range of earmarks for education-related initiatives.

The package also includes [a $500 million transfer from the Educational Opportunities Reserve Fund](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB237-enr.pdf) to support RAISE Act funding and the new CHEER Fund, which provides $65 million in performance-based funding for eligible colleges and universities.

# Could school districts' lawsuit change Wisconsin school funding system?

Days before the first deadline in a lawsuit aiming to dramatically shift [Wisconsin’s school funding system](https://www.greenbaypressgazette.com/story/news/education/2026/02/24/wisconsin-school-districts-sue-state-legislature-over-funding-system/88840612007/), much remains unsaid.

In late February, several school districts, teachers unions and parents filed a [lawsuit against the Wisconsin Legislature](https://www.greenbaypressgazette.com/story/news/education/2026/02/24/wisconsin-school-districts-sue-state-legislature-over-funding-system/88840612007/), alleging the state doesn’t provide enough funding for schools to meet constitutional requirements.

Defendant legislators had 45 days to respond, meaning the clock runs out April 13. As of April 8, legislators hadn't filed a response.

[Skip to content](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/missouri-lawmakers-discuss-school-funding/#main)

![](https://i0.wp.com/sgfcitizen.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/PXL_20260409_230438920.jpg?fit=780%2C585&ssl=1)Reps. Betsy Fogle, Stephanie Hein and Melanie Stinnett speak at a forum held Thursday at Glendale High School. (Photo by Joe Hadsall)

A forum about state education issues Thursday, April 9, in Springfield focused heavily on funding and the legislative struggle over ensuring public schools get enough.

Three Springfield-area members of the Missouri House of Representatives were the featured speakers in a panel at Glendale High School hosted by Springfield Public Schools, the Springfield NEA and Springfield chapter of the Missouri State Teachers Association.

Missouri Reps. Betsy Fogle, Stephanie Hein and Melanie Stinnett answered a variety of questions, most dealing with how schools are funded.

They addressed a number of initiatives that would have a significant effect, including changes to Missouri’s Foundation Formula, Gov. Mike Kehoe’s pitch to eliminate state income tax and continued public funding of MoScholars — Missouri’s voucher program that grants public money to pay private school tuition and fees.

About 150 people, some wearing logos representing suburban school districts across the metro area, attended the event.

## Preview of upcoming budget

The forum was held with about five weeks remaining in the legislative session. It was also held a couple of weeks after a school board meeting where board members got their first preview of the budget for the 2026-27 school year.

![](https://i0.wp.com/sgfcitizen.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/PXL_20260409_224625089.jpg?resize=780%2C585&ssl=1)Superintendent Grenita Lathan speaks about budget challenges for the 2026-27 school year. (Photo by Joe Hadsall)

Before the legislators spoke, Superintendent Grenita Lathan and Deputy Superintendent Travis Shaw shared details about the district’s anticipated revenues. The Springfield Board of Education in June will set the budget for the next school year.

The two showed a variety of conditions the district faces, including:

- A dwindling birth rate across the county and state.
- Lower numbers of school-aged students, pointing out that the number of high school graduates was roughly 170 more than the incoming class of kindergartners.
- The expectation of flat funding from the state and a reduction in transportation reimbursement.
- A non-assessment year, in which property taxes will remain flat.
- A reduced property tax collection rate because of a senior citizen tax freeze.

The two also emphasized that revenue estimates from the state change during the budgeting process.

“There are so many things that go into creating a budget,” Lathan said. “I encourage you to stay tuned and listen to our board meetings… (these) are decisions that we have to make moving forward, and why it’s important that we continue to communicate with our elected officials in Jefferson City.”

State funding accounted for almost 30% of the current school year’s budget.

SPS lobbyist Jason Zamkus also spoke about how the biggest issues facing the legislature that will have the biggest impact on schools are all budgetary.

“You have competing interests, whether they be property tax reform, income tax reform or a task force that’s looking at substantially overhauling the state’s Foundation Formula,” Zamkus said. “All of which seem to be, at times, moving in opposite directions.”

## Lawmakers answer variety of questions

[Stinnett, a Republican,](https://sgfcitizen.org/government/missouri-government-politics/recently-reelected-state-rep-melanie-stinnett-to-run-for-springfields-senate-seat-in-2026/) and [Fogle, a Democrat,](https://sgfcitizen.org/government/missouri-government-politics/springfield-state-rep-betsy-fogle-to-run-for-lincoln-houghs-state-senate-seat-in-2026/) are running for the District 30 State Senate seat currently held by Sen. Lincoln Hough, who will be term-limited in 2026. [Hein, a Democrat,](https://sgfcitizen.org/government/elections/springfield-area-election-candidates/) is running for her third term in the House.

All three were called “great friends of SPS,” and were praised for their responsiveness and ability to work across the aisle. Each of them spoke about a number of topics influencing schools, including some victories realized over the last few years. [Senate Bill 68](https://www.senate.mo.gov/25info/pdf-bill/tat/SB68.pdf) was named by Hein and Stinnett as an example of both sides working well together for a good bill.

They differed on two key issues, however — continued funding of MoScholars and immediate impacts of Kehoe’s state income tax elimination.

MoScholars offers money to parents for paying tuition and fees to private schools. Upon its creation, the money originally came from donors who were given tax credits.

But a lack of donors prompted Kehoe to authorize $51 million from the budget toward the program, transforming it into a true private-school voucher program. A review found that a large majority of those vouchers [went toward tuition in religious schools.](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/discovery-school-bucks-trend-but-almost-all-taxpayer-funded-scholarships-went-to-religious-schools/)

And the House approved a version of the bill that [increases that funding to $60 million.](https://sgfcitizen.org/government/missouri-government-politics/missouri-house-budget-approved/)

In a question about tracking the accountability of MoScholars funding toward student progress, all three said they favored such checks.

Stinnett said she supported the program, noting that the allocation accounts for .09% of the funding that goes toward education, and that the program helps fill a need for parents.

“For those of us who supported MoScholars, I think it’s important to say that doesn’t mean we are anti-public education,” said Stinnett, who is also a speech pathologist. “We want to support our public schools as well, but in my experience, I have had children I served in my clinic and in other pieces of my life that needed a different opportunity.”

Fogle said she reviewed many student handbooks of private schools receiving MoScholars money and found many of them can reject students for a variety of reasons.

“I can’t think of anything less American than that,” Fogle said. “I think we live in a country where every child should have access to a free and quality public education system. If we continue to go down this path where only some children are deemed worthy, or only some children can afford education, I am very concerned by that.”

Hein emphasized accountability for how MoScholars funds are spent through accreditation and more.

“We ask our public schools to do so much, and we are continually adding on to our public schools,” Hein said. “At some point, if you are starting to take tax dollars in your private school, you are going to need to be able to do those same things with our money.”

## State income tax elimination

The three also shared thoughts about [Kehoe’s plan to eliminate the state income tax,](https://sgfcitizen.org/government/missouri-government-politics/governor-kehoe-proposes-missouri-income-tax-phaseout/) if voters approve.

Such an elimination is expected to result in the loss of as much as $9 billion, Fogle said.

“I think we need to be very careful about passing a bill that has absolutely no budget wrapped around it, and doesn’t tell the voter how much your sales tax is going to increase,” Fogle said. “There are some parts in the bill that address public education at the local level, but my concern is about general revenue, and how much we invest at the state level.”

Hein noted that the biggest targets for budget cuts are public education, higher education and social services such as Medicaid.

“They take the brunt of any revenue loss that we have,” Hein said. “If we see these cuts happen, we are going to see implications across our communities, not just our public schools.”

Stinnett said that the bill has triggers that will prevent those dire funding losses, in order to ensure a funding replacement.

“If we don’t increase revenue, then the income tax remains just as it is,” Stinnett said. “If we spend a few years trying to figure out how to adjust or change those sales taxes, then nothing would happen, so it’s an opportunity for us to try and see what we could do. But first, we have to get permission from you all to determine that.”

![](https://www.pressherald.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/04/43537162_20260409_EPS_5251.jpg?w=1200)Committee clerks pass out papers during an Education and Cultural Affairs meeting Thursday for a language review of a bill to reform Maine's school funding formula. (Joe Phelan/Staff Photographer)

Lawmakers made last-minute changes Thursday to a bill that would reform Maine’s fraught school funding formula after a fiscal note on the cost came back $25 million higher than expected.

The Education and Cultural Affairs Committee initially passed [LD 2226](https://legislature.maine.gov/billtracker/#Paper/2226?legislature=132) with broad support last month but agreed to review the language and consider amendments in an effort to bring potential costs down.

The amended version passed by a 10-2 margin, but some Republican lawmakers raised concerns about feeling rushed in the process. It now goes to the full Legislature.

The bill as amended makes major changes to Maine’s Essential Programs and Services formula, commonly known as EPS, that school leaders for years have argued is outdated and inequitable. The changes wouldn’t take effect until the 2027-28 fiscal year and are not a part of the ongoing state budget process.

In 2024, the education committee asked a nonpartisan research group to study and propose changes to the formula. That group, the Maine Educational Policy Research Institute, [returned a report over the summer](https://www.pressherald.com/2025/08/10/maines-school-funding-formula-has-long-been-called-inequitable-changing-it-is-complicated/), which lawmakers then [adapted into a committee bill](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/04/lawmakers-draft-overhaul-of-maines-scrutinized-school-funding-formula/). Two of its most significant provisions would integrate a district’s rate of economically disadvantaged students into the formula (rather than relying entirely on property tax valuations), and update an outdated model of regional salary adjustments.

The changes outlined in the amended bill will result in higher state subsidies for 247 of the state’s 262 school districts.

Advertisement

School leaders from around the state [showed support for the bill](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/09/maine-school-district-leaders-agree-funding-formula-update-is-overdue/) during a public hearing, but had some concerns. The committee made several changes in response, which included removing any adjustments to the special education portion of the formula. Lawmakers also amended the bill to delay implementation until 2031 for school districts that will get less from the state.

Rep. Michael Brennan, D-Portland, said Thursday the committee expected the cost of the bill to be around $45 million, so members were shocked when it was closer to $70 million.

The increase originated from some provisions that were left over from an original version of the bill, including a change related to transportation payments, as well as a calculation error. Brennan submitted an amendment to remove the transportation language and address other issues, which would bring the total fiscal impact back down to $45 million, a legislative analyst said.

[![](https://www.pressherald.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/04/43537162_20260409_EPS_5195.jpg?w=1024)](https://w2pcms.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/10/2026/04/43537162_20260409_EPS_5195.jpg) Rep. Michael Brennan, D-Portland, speaks during an education committee meeting for a language review on LD 2226. (Joe Phelan/Staff Photographer)[Purchase this image](https://dev.mainetodaymedia.com/smugmug/upload.php?data=%7B%22src%22%3A%22https%3A%5C%2F%5C%2Fwww.pressherald.com%5C%2Fwp-content%5C%2Fuploads%5C%2Fsites%5C%2F4%5C%2F2026%5C%2F04%5C%2F43537162_20260409_EPS_5195.jpg%22%2C%22caption%22%3A%22Rep.%20Michael%20Brennan%2C%20D-Portland%2C%20speaks%20during%20an%20education%20committee%20meeting%20for%20a%20language%20review%20on%20LD%202226.%20%28Joe%20Phelan%5C%2FStaff%20Photographer%29%22%7D)

“It can be overwhelming, but I would stand very firmly in a place that this amendment is very reflective of the majority opinion and discussion of this committee,” Brennan said.

The meeting turned animated at times as minority committee members said they felt that the changes were rushed, and they wouldn’t be able to sell them to their caucus. Rep. Barbara Bagshaw, R-Windham, and Sen. James Libby, R-Cumberland, each voted no.

Co-Chair Kelly Murphy, D-Scarborough, encouraged the committee to move the bill forward.

Advertisement

“The two changes that we are making are the first changes in 20 years, (and) will make a significant benefit for two-thirds of the students of Maine,” she said, emphasizing that the amendment did not add any new material, only removed costs.

School leaders around the state have been eagerly awaiting passage of LD 2226 as they deal with their own budget processes, which [have been especially tough this year](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/18/its-a-tough-budget-year-for-maines-school-districts-why/).

Robbie Feinberg, spokesperson for the Maine School Superintendents Association, testified Thursday at the request of the committee, and said the latest amendment had the support of his members.

“We feel that this amendment is a very strong step forward,” he said.

# Letters, Week of April 8, 2026: School funding, PeaceHealth cuts, idling train engines

## Send letters, maximum 250 words, to letters@cascadiadaily.com

- April 7, 2026 9:00 p.m.

By [Community Voices](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/author/community-voices/)

# LETTER OF THE WEEK

### Lawmakers have defied courts for decades on K-12 funding

![](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/unnamed-2-2048x1365-1-1024x683.jpg)Washington state lawmakers in the House chamber on the first day of the 2026 legislative session. (Photo courtesy of Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)

##### Editor,

As a Washington school district superintendent for 25 years, I dealt with the state’s inadequate funding models that shifted funding burdens to school districts dependent on voters’ approval of increased local taxes.

Superior Court Judge Robert Doran ruled in 1978 that Washington’s school funding model did not comply with Article IX of our state’s Constitution: “It is the paramount duty of the state to make ample provision for the education of all children residing within its borders” (ample defined as _enough_).

Doran ruled in 1984 that attempts to provide “ample funding” didn’t meet the terms of his 1978 decision. More legislative attempts did not satisfy the mandates of the state constitution and Doran’s decisions. The State Supreme Court’s 2012 McCleary decision ruled that the state’s school funding didn’t comply with Article IX.

More attempts failed and resulted in a contempt ruling in 2014 and a $100,000 a day fine to be paid by the Legislature. The Legislature did comply with the McCleary ruling in 2018; 40 years after the first Doran decision.

The 2026 Legislature and the governor have approved school funding that may again violate Article IX. If so, local voters will be asked to pay more taxes and court cases will likely ensue and likely will prevail. When will lawmakers conform to their oath of office rather than being held in contempt (again) as a result of one or more court decisions? Will it take another 40 years for the Legislature and the governor to comply with Washington’s constitution?

##### Jerry Hunter  Bellingham

##### Editor,

The Bellingham School District’s decision to cut 60 teaching positions ( [CDN, April 1, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/01/no-elementary-schools-will-close-before-2027-bellingham-superintendent-says/)) is deeply concerning. While we all understand that budget constraints require difficult choices, eliminating educators, especially those in critical roles such as librarians and mental health counselors, should be a last resort, not a first step.

Teachers and student support staff are the backbone of our schools. They work directly with students every day, shaping not only academic outcomes but also emotional well-being and long-term success. Removing these positions will have a lasting impact on the quality of education and support our students receive.

Before making cuts that directly affect students, the district should take a closer look at other areas of spending. This includes administrative growth, outside consulting contracts and costly technology subscriptions that may not be fully utilized. Large curriculum adoptions, such as the International Baccalaureate program, should also be reevaluated. IB is expensive and has not clearly demonstrated strong positive results for the broader student population, raising questions about whether it is the right investment during a budget crisis.

Additionally, the district should evaluate whether certain universal programs could be better targeted to those most in need. Programs like Project Free Education, which provide school supplies for all students regardless of financial need, may be well-intentioned but deserve review to ensure resources are being used as efficiently as possible while still supporting equity goals.

This is not about eliminating valuable programs; it is about prioritizing what matters most. In times of budget shortfalls, our first responsibility should be to protect the people who serve students face-to-face every day.

Bellingham’s students deserve classrooms staffed with the educators and support professionals who help them thrive. Let’s make sure our budget reflects that priority.

##### Brad Jones  Bellingham

##### Editor,

I was very disappointed to hear that in the budget for the next school year, the Bellingham School District has chosen to eliminate all of the certificated library positions in elementary, middle and high schools ( [CDN, April 1, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/01/no-elementary-schools-will-close-before-2027-bellingham-superintendent-says/)). They would like you to believe that replacing those positions with non-certificated employees will mean that the libraries in our schools will remain open and students will have access to reading materials and resources.

What is really happening is that they have chosen to completely cut the programs that teach students how to use those resources. Librarians teach students how to gather information from authentic resources, how to verify that their sources are legitimate, and how to present that information. In these days when misinformation abounds, we need our students to learn the skills that will enable them to make informed and intelligent decisions.

Librarians in our schools are also the leaders in schools in promoting independent reading, guiding choices and introducing readers to literature for children and teens. Librarians select books based on the interests and reading abilities of students in their schools. Cutting those positions will leave one district librarian to select books for all of the schools without knowing what those students need.

I know that the district is faced with making some difficult decisions about budget cuts, but I believe that cutting librarians is the wrong direction if we want our children to become responsible, literate adults.

##### Scout Mitchell  Bellingham

##### Editor,

Regarding PeaceHealth Northwest official Charles Prosper’s statement about Advanced Care Planning (ACP), now that the ACP staffing has been eliminated system wide ( [CDN, April 3, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/03/peacehealth-were-working-to-adapt-and-evolve-to-funding-shifts-amid-community-angst/)), “Yes, we have made changes in the methodology and how we’re going about it, but we are not giving up in ensuring that those services are still delivered to our patients.” I decided to call PeaceHealth to find out how I could update my Advanced Care Directive. I was transferred to records; they did not know the answer to the question (and) referred me to the webpage for ACP. At the bottom of that page, a note: utilization was low, and the decision was made to eliminate staff. ACP “is integrated into routine care across our ambulatory settings.”

As a PeaceHealth volunteer, I’ve gone through ACD training with Hilary Walker to promote and support the greater adoption of Advance Care Directives. I have taken part in the community ACP workshops with other volunteers and staff supporting patients to understand the process and to help them make decisions. The process is not as simple as deciding to declare oneself as DNR (do not resuscitate).

Providers, who are already burdened, do not have the time nor the expertise to advise their patients on ACP during an exam. If it’s true that utilization was low, it’s all the more reason why there needs to be more support for champions within the system who are promoting ACP. Hilary Walker was one of those champions. Everything Prosper said was true; what was left out from his explanation is the true impact of the loss of the ACP program, which is huge.

##### Morgan Bruce Hostetter  Bellingham

##### Editor,

Thanks to Executive Editor Ron Judd for his recent piece on Rick Steves, his warnings about creeping fascism and encouraging Americans to travel abroad ( [CDN, April 2, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/02/rick-steves-has-new-advice-for-americans-and-its-not-about-packing-your-bags/)). Travel is a great chance for each of us to become ambassadors of our country.

Another way to prevent this destruction of our democracy has been shown by millions of people around the country, taking a stand against what is going on, like the recent No Kings Day. Another way to influence our democracy is by speaking up to those who represent us in Congress. Both Sens. Maria Cantwell and Patty Murray, along with Reps. Rick Larsen and Suzan DelBene are good listeners and extremely concerned about the actions of the current administration. We can thank them and encourage them to keep working to turn back things like the tax gift to the wealthy on the backs of the poor.

People are hungry and unable to afford health insurance and rent. Our voices can help change that.

##### Willie Dickerson   Snohomish

##### Editor,

Nothing we can do. Fences. These are the solutions we have heard so far. The people living in the camps and the people surviving in the alleys have no pathways. The homeowners, business owners and residents are left with questions. And frustration. The connection is the people in the camps and the alleyways. They need a hand.

The connection is King Mountain residents, the downtown business owners and downtown patrons. They deserve solutions. Their tax dollars should buy solutions. People in elected positions, law enforcement and especially our overworked and underpaid social service providers should get together and problem solve.  Robust support of treatment and housing facilities, ordinances and responsible police presence to curb criminal behavior are answers.

To those who say “get a job” and “take responsibility,” you dismiss the addiction, the PTSD and the untreated behavioral health complications. To those who say the heroic efforts of our social service providers and the intervention and diversion teams who work tirelessly to help are the problem, I ask that you just say thank you. And support them.

There are no answers that are going to satisfy everyone. We have a shortage of funding from the federal and state level to immediately improve transitional housing development. Our old and decrepit jail is full.  Our new jail project must have public support for holistic rehabilitative treatments, addiction treatment and life skills education. Start somewhere, but please start.

##### Kevin Stray  Bellingham

##### Editor,

The April 3, 2026, issue of The Seattle Times has a front-page article headlined “Washington’s timber industry feels like it’s on the chopping block.” Administration-fueled trade wars, reciprocal tariffs, a tariffs-shocked stock market, the unlawful Iran war, a politicized export market that “kind of went away,” climbing interest rates, skyrocketing utility costs, increasing transport (diesel) costs, falling lumber prices, and relentlessly increasing manufacturing costs, are among its leading causes.

Meanwhile, the grifter-in-chief, his family and his oligarch associates are benefiting from the chaos he creates and are raking in the cash. Many timber industry owners, managers and financiers voted for this self-proclaimed “genius” in 2024, whose ill-considered policies and actions underlie the slowing economy and troubled marketplace.

Any voter remorse yet?

##### Curt Wolters  Bellingham

##### Editor,

I wonder how many people realize how long locomotives idle in this country; not minutes or hours, but days. I live in Sumas, overlooking a rail yard. For five straight days, a locomotive has sat below my home, running nonstop. No crew. No activity. Just a low, constant hum filling the air.

The industry has its reasons: keeping engines warm, enabling quick starts and maintaining crew comfort. Fair enough. But what’s striking is the lack of meaningful oversight. Despite being widespread, locomotive idling isn’t consistently tracked or regulated. We’re expected to accept that massive diesel engines run indefinitely in our communities.

That’s hard to justify when solutions already exist: batteries, auxiliary power units, electrification. These aren’t futuristic ideas; they’re proven technologies. Yet adoption lags.

The cost is real. A locomotive burns roughly 3 to 5 gallons of diesel per hour at idle; thousands of dollars a week for an engine doing nothing. Multiply that nationwide, and the waste becomes staggering. Add emissions — carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter — and the impact on air quality and public health becomes clear.

But the most immediate effect is the noise. Not loud, but relentless. A low rumble that seeps into homes and lingers day and night. It’s not dramatic; it’s constant, and that’s what makes it worse.

This isn’t complicated. Idle limits, cleaner technology and accountability are all achievable.

If this is what progress sounds like, we should ask why it still sounds like 1950.

##### Rich Kohr  Sumas

##### Editor,

PeaceHealth’s April 2 community forum left mixed impressions ( [CDN, April 3, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/03/peacehealth-were-working-to-adapt-and-evolve-to-funding-shifts-amid-community-angst/)). They allotted just 15 minutes for Q&A, a brief, highly controlled window in a conversation that deserved more openness.

Yet one moment shone clearly. When PeaceHealth’s Rachel Lucy spoke of “social drivers of health,” her words, for me, carried respect and optimism.

For years, public health discussions have been framed around “social determinants of health,” a phrase that can sound final, as if people’s circumstances determine their outcomes. By choosing “drivers,” Lucy shifted that meaning toward possibility rather than inevitability, suggesting that communities can influence the conditions that shape their well‑being.

In contrast, PeaceHealth management invoked language such as “adapt and evolve” to justify cutting valued programs, among them Advance Care Planning and clinical social worker positions. Framed as progress, that rhetoric can ring hollow when the effect is fewer human connections and supports for patients, families and medical providers.

Adapt and evolve can sound like a one‑way directive, as if those who can’t adjust to top‑down changes are simply left behind. True adaptation in health care should mean evolving with our community, not away from it. When language honors shared purpose, as Lucy’s did, it feels inclusive and genuine.

One attendee viewed PeaceHealth’s “adaptation” as trimming critical services that already operate on thin margins as the new euphemism for “we do not want to try anything harder than firing people. Yet, top executives get regular raises to their million-dollar-plus salaries.”

##### Micki Jackson  Bellingham

##### Editor,

The largest proposed housing developments in Whatcom County are in Blaine, yet there is no news coverage. Two planned unit developments at Birch Point of roughly 500 homes each would flood their downhill neighbors in Birch Bay Village, a gated community of 1,000 homes. The first phase of a 568-unit manufactured home park in East Blaine is now being challenged as a threat to the public water system, which serves 17,000 customers in Blaine and Birch Bay. Watch the [Water Planning Matters video](https://www.waterplanningmatters.org/creeksidewaterrisks) and read the complaint to the Washington State Department of Health.

##### Jay Taber  Blaine

##### Editor,

I am a retired family nurse practitioner who has spent my career working in nonprofit and public health settings, and I was among those who signed the community letter regarding the decision of the PeaceHealth corporate leadership to eliminate clinical social work positions vital to the Center for Senior Health, the Cancer Center and Whatcom Hospice, along with dismantling the Advance Care Planning program.

In reviewing the excellent investigative reporting by Owen Racer ( [CDN, April 3, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/03/peacehealth-were-working-to-adapt-and-evolve-to-funding-shifts-amid-community-angst/)) as well as information available online detailing the compensation of the PeaceHealth executive team, I am struck by the fact that more than 15 members of that team have earned between $1 million and $2 million annually.

Taking the median figure of $1.5 million pencils out to more than $720 an hour, while the salary range for a PeaceHealth clinical social worker with an MSW is $46.27 to $69.41 an hour.

Rounding up and paying those with a master’s of social work a generous $70 an hour, a cutback equivalent to one hour of the PeaceHealth executive team members’ compensation would pay for more than 154 hours of social work services.

To me, this seems like a reasonable alternative to the cuts made by the PeaceHealth organization, and I join with other involved community members in calling for PeaceHealth to immediately reinstate all eliminated social work and Advance Care Planning positions.

##### Margaret Jahn  Bellingham

##### Editor,

We have far more in common than what divides us. If we share a commitment to the Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the rule of law, truth over lies and treating others as we’d want to be treated, how far apart are we really? We might disagree on funding or priority, but not on the values themselves.

And yet politicians on all sides work overtime to convince us that the other half of the country is the enemy, because keeping us divided, off balance and scared is their fundraising model.

I’d love to see a march of American citizens — not Democrats, not Republicans, just citizens — sending a unified message to every elected official: Honor what you swore to uphold, or we’ll replace you.

I did march in the No Kings Rally last Sunday, not for any party, but in protest of how badly this administration violates those principles. That said, others before it have as well. If we don’t address the underlying dysfunction, nothing fundamentally changes. Democrats may win the midterms — and then what? The war continues with different generals.

We need to remember: these politicians work for us. We hire them, give them a job description and evaluate them at the ballot box. We recognize no kings. Until we stop outsourcing our civic identity to parties that refuse to address term limits, election reform, gerrymandering and voter suppression, we’ll keep mistaking a change of power for actual progress.

It’s not too late. But it’s past time we took the reins.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

##### Tom Otten  Bellingham

##### Editor,

My heart goes out to all the brave men and women who are voluntarily serving in our armed forces.  The toll this latest war will have on them mentally and physically will last for years, if not a lifetime.

We are still trying to figure out how to care for those affected by the long deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan, where, in addition to the mental stress, they breathed in all sorts of nasty burning chemicals as oil wells and refineries were set ablaze. Iran’s Kharg Island will be a toxic mess for our Marines to fight and live through.

Many of those currently in the region have arrived stressed from already long deployments. The USS Gerald R. Ford has been at sea for almost 270 days. In mid-April, it will break the record for the longest carrier deployment since the Vietnam War.

We don’t seem to be able to stop this administration from going to war, but let’s try to make sure they care for those who fought it when and if they finally get home.

##### Gary P. Malick  Bellingham

##### Editor,

Curiously, the framers of the American Constitution counted on a social deposit of civic responsibility. But we no longer can. Instead, we have a president and government corrupting our way of life.

We are living in a fractured country; more and more, we confront one another as aggrieved groups rather than as a unified democracy. While it was a powerful feeling on March 28 when our community’s energy shifted from a shared sentiment to a collective movement, now the work — ballots and pens — is what actually moves the needle. Writing letters or organizing phone banks turns that community spirit into measurable data.

##### Helen Moran  Bellingham

# Opinion: The business case for adjusting school funding for inflation and passing Prop 9

By Adam Hays, Steph Johnson and Patrick Lovelace

Published: April 4, 2026

![](https://www.adn.com/resizer/v2/6I4EA4DM6NAPTJFPBZXRIFNMGQ.jpg?auth=cc8bd50977f0ee96ab390ede7107414800316fbbccf332b39eb78197516ac13b&width=800&height=533)(iStock / Getty Images)

As business owners, we look at Anchorage through the lens of long-term viability. We invest in our storefronts, our fleets and our employees because we believe in this city’s future. But lately, that future is looking increasingly fragile.

For seven years, we’ve watched a slow-motion crisis in our schools that is now hitting our bottom lines. When neighborhood schools like [Fire Lake or Lake Otis](https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/education/2026/02/25/anchorage-school-board-passes-budget-with-closures-and-significant-staff-cuts/ "https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/education/2026/02/25/anchorage-school-board-passes-budget-with-closures-and-significant-staff-cuts/") close, property values shift and local commerce patterns break. When class sizes balloon and programs like IGNITE are axed, the families we employ start looking for the exit. We aren’t just losing students; we are losing our current workforce and failing to develop our future one.

To stabilize our economy and our community, we believe Anchorage must pursue a two-track solution: a state funding inflation adjustment and local support for [Proposition 9](https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/anchorage/2026/02/22/heres-what-bonds-to-expect-on-anchorages-upcoming-municipal-election-ballot/ "https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/anchorage/2026/02/22/heres-what-bonds-to-expect-on-anchorages-upcoming-municipal-election-ballot/").

The math is simple: You cannot run a 2026 business on a 2017 budget. Between skyrocketing costs for utilities, insurance and labor, “flat funding” is, in reality, a massive budget cut.

Recent data reveals a startling trend: [Alaska ranks last among all 50 states](https://edunomicslab.org/roi-over-time/ "https://edunomicslab.org/roi-over-time/") in cumulative spending growth per pupil relative to inflation. While the rest of the country adjusted to a 35% inflation rate, Alaska limped along at just 14%. We are starving our competitive edge.

Fortunately, many of our legislators in Juneau see the crisis we are facing and are taking action. The House Education Committee has introduced [House Bill 374](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/Bill/Text/34?Hsid=HB0374A# "https://www.akleg.gov/basis/Bill/Text/34?Hsid=HB0374A#") to adjust the Base Student Allocation, or BSA, to restore some of the investment lost to inflation. The Senate Education Committee has introduced [Senate Bill 277](https://legiscan.com/AK/bill/SB277/2025 "https://legiscan.com/AK/bill/SB277/2025") to modestly increase the BSA and introduce a suite of policy reforms and funding measures designed to build consensus and make targeted investments. We are grateful for this leadership.

This isn’t about “more” money; it’s about restoring the purchasing power necessary to keep our schools functional. We need a predictable funding formula so businesses and families can plan for the future with confidence.

ADVERTISEMENT

While we support the work happening in Juneau, we cannot leave our classrooms unprotected. Even if a state adjustment passes, it won’t undo years of structural damage overnight. Proposition 9 is our local insurance policy.

Proposition 9 is a one-time, $11.8 million levy dedicated solely to retaining more than 80 teacher positions. Without it, the Anchorage School District will be forced to increase the pupil-teacher ratio by four students per class.

From a business perspective, the return on investment here is clear:

• Small cost: For a $400,000 property, the cost is roughly $9 a month.

ADVERTISEMENT

• High impact: It prevents catastrophic classroom overcrowding that drives young professional families to leave the state.

• Stability: It is a one-year rescue mission, not a permanent tax hike. It buys us the time needed for the state to fix the funding formula without losing more talent in the process.

We cannot recruit top-tier talent to Anchorage if our school system is in a state of managed decline. We cannot build a robust economy on the back of a systematic erosion of public education driven by years of vetoes and stagnant funding.

As employers, we know that investing in our schools is investing in our local economy. On April 7, join us in voting yes on Proposition 9 and demanding a real inflation adjustment from Juneau. Let’s stop the bleeding and give Anchorage a fighting chance to thrive.

_**Adam Hays**_ _,_ _**Steph Johnson**_ _and_ _**Patrick Lovelace**_ _are each Anchorage business owners._

![](https://dailydodge.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Andrew-Hysell-photo.jpg)

(MADISON ) Tuesday is Spring Election Day in Wisconsin. 60 school districts will hold operational referendums, asking voters to exceed state-imposed spending limits by a total of more than $1billion.

Meanwhile, Democrats have introduced a bill in the state assembly to increase state spending on schools to 60% of costs.

“This is while the state is sitting on a ($2.5 billion) surplus,” State Rep. Andrew Hysell (D-Sun Prairie) told Daily Dodge. “It’s ridiculous that state politicians can pat themselves on the back for a surplus, while they’re starving our local communities and schools.”

Republican legislative leaders and Democratic Governor Tony Evers are negotiating their own deal on school funding and tax relief. Lawmakers are expected to meet in April in an extraordinary session to consider it.
